Short version: **start on the Free plan today; the drip design eventually needs a paid plan + the Transactional add-on.** Here's the mapping to phases (pricing as of my knowledge — worth a 2-minute check on mailchimp.com since they reshuffle tiers):

**Phase 1 — collect the list (now).** Free plan: ~500 contacts, ~1,000 sends/month. Signup forms, the embedded-form action URL our `NewsletterSignup.vue` posts to, double opt-in, unsubscribe handling, and full API access are all included. Since you want the list growing from day one but aren't sending yet, this costs nothing and unblocks pasting `MAILCHIMP_ACTION`.

**Phase 2 — the per-subscriber drip.** This is the part regular Marketing plans don't cover well, because their send quotas and tools are built around *campaigns* (one email → many people), while our oldest-unsent design is *individualized* sends (each subscriber may get a different post on the same day). That's transactional-style sending, which is **Mailchimp Transactional (Mandrill)** — an add-on bought in blocks of **25,000 emails ≈ $20/month**, on top of a paid Marketing plan (cheapest is Essentials, ~$13/month at 500 contacts, scaling with list size).

Math check on one block: at an every-other-day cadence each subscriber gets ~15 emails/month, so 25k emails ≈ **1,600 subscribers** — one block carries you a long way. So realistic steady-state cost once the drip is live: **~$33/month** until the list gets seriously big.

The Free plan's 1,000 sends/month, for contrast, would only cover ~65 drip subscribers — fine for a soft launch experiment, not for the real thing.

**One honest alternative to price-check before committing to Phase 2:** keep Mailchimp free as the signup/audience layer, and point the Worker's delivery at **Resend** (3,000 emails/month free, then $20/month for 50k) instead of Mandrill. Same architecture, same ledger, roughly half the cost — the tradeoff is you sync unsubscribes between two systems instead of one, which is exactly the kind of glue that erodes. If you'd rather never think about suppression-list sync, pay for the all-Mailchimp stack.

Recommendation: create the free account now, paste the form URL, grow the list. Decide Mandrill vs Resend when the list is big enough that Phase 2 is real — you'll know the actual subscriber count and can price it precisely instead of guessing.

does free plan have mandrill too in mailchimp?

No — Mandrill isn't part of the free plan. Mailchimp Transactional is a paid add-on, and to buy the email blocks (~$20 per 25k/month) you need a paid Mailchimp Marketing plan under it. As I recall there's only a **demo/trial** of Transactional available otherwise — a few hundred test sends, restricted to email addresses on domains you've verified as your own, so it's enough to build and test the Worker → Mandrill integration but not to send to real subscribers.

So the practical ladder is:

1. **Free plan now** — signup form live, list grows, no sending. $0.
2. **When the drip goes live** — either Essentials (~$13/mo) + one Transactional block (~$20/mo) for the all-Mailchimp stack, or Mailchimp free + Resend for delivery (free to 3k emails/month) if you accept syncing unsubscribes across two systems.

One extra note on the trial being domain-restricted: that's actually convenient for us — you can verify ivue.dev, seed the ledger with a few test addresses of your own, and dry-run the whole cron → oldest-unsent → send pipeline end-to-end for free before a single dollar or real subscriber is involved.

any other alternative to mailchimp or you think it's best?

Mailchimp isn't sacred here — and honestly, the drip design we converged on *changed the requirements* in a way that weakens my earlier Mailchimp recommendation. That recommendation was strongest when Mailchimp's built-in machinery (RSS campaigns, journeys) was doing the work. But we've since decided the scheduling brain lives in your own Worker ledger, which demotes the platform to three jobs: hosted signup/consent, a suppression list, and an API that delivers individual emails. Once those are the requirements, API-first services do it cheaper and cleaner. The real field:

| Service | Free tier | Fit for the ledger design |
|---|---|---|
| **Brevo** (ex-Sendinblue) | 300 emails/day, unlimited contacts, transactional API included | Marketing + transactional in **one system**, one suppression list — the all-in-one Mailchimp promise, but the transactional half is free |
| **Resend** | 3,000 emails/month | Best developer experience of the lot; audiences + unsubscribe handling included now, but it's delivery-first — thinner audience UI |
| **Buttondown / Kit / MailerLite** | varies (MailerLite: 1k subs) | Newsletter-shaped, good UIs, but their automations are fixed sequences — same mismatch with oldest-unsent as Mailchimp journeys |
| **Postmark / Amazon SES** | SES ≈ $0.10 per 1,000 | Pure pipes, superb deliverability (SES cheapest by far), but zero audience layer — you own compliance entirely |
| **Mailchimp** | 500 contacts, 1k sends/mo | Polished audience layer, but the drip needs Mandrill = paid plan + $20 blocks, ~$33/mo at your scale |

**My actual pick for your design: Brevo, with Resend as the close second.** Brevo's free tier (300/day ≈ 9,000 emails/month) covers roughly **600 subscribers on an every-other-day drip for $0**, with signup forms, GDPR consent, unsubscribe pages, and the transactional API all sharing one suppression list — no cross-system sync, which was the one real cost of the Resend hybrid. Resend wins if you value API ergonomics and a cleaner dashboard over the bundled marketing UI, and its MCP story is arguably the best (dev-first docs, simple REST an agent can't misuse much).

Two practical notes:

- **The form change is trivial.** Our `NewsletterSignup.vue` posts Mailchimp-style JSONP, which is Mailchimp-specific — but the moment a Worker exists, the form should post to *your* Worker endpoint anyway (Worker → provider API + writes the ledger). That makes the provider a swappable line item behind your own URL, which is exactly where you want it: switch Brevo → Resend → SES later without touching the site.
- **When Mailchimp still wins:** if you decide the Worker ledger is more machinery than you want and fall back to "just email new posts + a fixed welcome sequence," Mailchimp's polish and RSS campaigns earn their price again. The platform choice follows the architecture choice.

So: keep the free Mailchimp account only if you want its form live *this week* while deciding. If you're committed to the ledger drip, start on Brevo and skip the migration entirely.

# ivue newsletter Worker

Subscribe endpoint + send ledger (D1) + daily drip cron. Brevo holds the
contact list and delivers email; this Worker decides who gets what, when.

**The invariant:** at most one email per (subscriber, post), ever. The
`sends` table is the invariant; the drip picks each subscriber's **oldest
unsent** post, so an ad-hoc `/broadcast` today can never be repeated by the
drip later — there is no exclusion logic, just the ledger.

Cadence: one email per subscriber at most every `CADENCE_HOURS` (default
40h ≈ every other day). A broadcast counts as that day's email.

## One-time setup

1. **Brevo account** (free: 300 emails/day) at brevo.com

   - Create a contact list; put its numeric id in `wrangler.jsonc` →
     `BREVO_LIST_ID` (Contacts → Lists — the id is in the URL).
   - Verify the sending domain (Senders & Domains → add `ivue.dev`, set the
     DKIM/DMARC DNS records it shows — Cloudflare DNS, 5 minutes).
   - Create an API key (SMTP & API → API keys).

2. **Create the database and apply the schema** (from this directory):

   ```sh
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 d1 create ivue-newsletter
   #   → paste the printed database_id into wrangler.jsonc
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 d1 execute ivue-newsletter --remote --file=schema.sql
   ```

3. **Secrets:**

   ```sh
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 secret put BREVO_API_KEY
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 secret put ADMIN_SECRET   # long random string
   ```

4. **Deploy** (wrangler pinned — see LESSONS.md on 4.121.0):

   ```sh
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 deploy
   ```

   Paste the printed `*.workers.dev` URL into `wrangler.jsonc` →
   `WORKER_ORIGIN` and deploy once more (unsubscribe links embed it).

5. **Point the site form at the Worker:** set `NEWSLETTER_ENDPOINT` in
   `docs_v2/.vitepress/theme/components/NewsletterSignup.vue` to the same
   URL, rebuild, deploy the site.

## Verify before real subscribers

Subscribe with your own address via the site form (or curl), then force a
drip pass instead of waiting for the cron:

```sh
curl -X POST "$WORKER/subscribe" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Evgeny","email":"user@example.com"}'
npx wrangler@4.120.1 triggers deploy   # or: dashboard → Trigger cron
```

Check that the email arrives, the **unsubscribe link resolves** (params
substitution in `htmlContent` — the one Brevo behavior worth an eyeball),
and the ledger recorded it:

```sh
npx wrangler@4.120.1 d1 execute ivue-newsletter --remote \
  --command='SELECT * FROM sends'
```

## Ad-hoc broadcast (also the future MCP tool surface)

```sh
curl -X POST "$WORKER/broadcast" \
  -H "authorization: [redacted]" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"slug":"circular-imports-dissolved"}'
```

Sends that post now to everyone who never received it, writes the ledger,
and reports `{recipients, skippedAsRepeat}`.

## How the drip finds posts

The site build emits `https://ivue.dev/blog-index.json`
(`docs_v2/scripts/blog-index-generator.mjs`, chained into `build:docs`) —
slugs, titles, descriptions, dates, sorted oldest-first. Publishing a post
requires no Worker change: it appears in the index, and everyone who is
caught up receives it as their next drip email.

Done — the Worker + Brevo system is built and committed (`2b0f959`). What exists now:

**`newsletter/` — the Worker** (`wrangler.jsonc`, `schema.sql`, `src/index.mjs`, `README.md`)
- **The ledger is the design**: a D1 `sends` table keyed `(email, slug)` — the invariant from our discussion made literal. The daily 13:00 UTC cron gives each due subscriber their **oldest unsent** post; `POST /broadcast {slug}` sends a post to everyone *now* and writes the same ledger, so the drip structurally can't repeat it. A broadcast also counts as that day's email (40h cadence var ≈ every other day).
- `POST /subscribe` creates the Brevo contact (CORS-locked to ivue.dev); `GET /unsubscribe` is HMAC-token-signed, writes a local suppression row *first* and mirrors into Brevo best-effort — so an unsubscribe holds even if the Brevo call fails.
- Sends are batched per-slug through Brevo's `messageVersions` (≤ a few dozen subrequests per cron no matter the list size — safely inside the Workers free plan's 50/invocation cap). A failed batch leaves the ledger unwritten, so it retries next run instead of losing people.

**Blog index** — new `sync:blog-index` step in `build:docs` emits `https://ivue.dev/blog-index.json` (32 posts, oldest-first, title/description/date/url). Publishing a post needs zero Worker changes — caught-up subscribers just receive it as their next drip email.

**The form** — `NewsletterSignup.vue` now posts JSON to `NEWSLETTER_ENDPOINT` (Mailchimp JSONP removed). Empty string keeps today's dormant soft-fail behavior, so nothing changes on the live site until you're ready.

**Your key-turns** are all in `newsletter/README.md`: Brevo account + list id + domain DKIM + API key, `d1 create` (paste the id), two secrets, deploy, paste the Worker URL into `WORKER_ORIGIN` and `NEWSLETTER_ENDPOINT`. All commands pinned to `wrangler@4.120.1` per LESSONS. One thing to eyeball on your first self-test send: that Brevo substitutes `{{params.UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}` inside inline `htmlContent` — the README's verify section walks through it; if it ever doesn't, tell me and I'll switch to per-recipient rendering.

The `/broadcast` endpoint is also deliberately the future MCP tool surface — "send this post now" is one authorized call that keeps the invariant.

parts.text: what is inbox placement?

Inbox placement is *where* a delivered email actually lands — the inbox, or the spam folder (or Gmail's Promotions tab). It's the metric that matters more than "delivery rate," and providers love to blur the two:

- **Delivery rate** counts emails the receiving server *accepted*. An email that gets accepted and silently filed into spam still counts as "delivered." Providers advertising 99% delivery are telling you almost nothing.
- **Inbox placement** counts emails that reached the folder a human actually looks at. This is the number that decides whether your newsletter gets read.

What determines it: the receiving side (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo) scores every message on sender reputation — the sending IP's history, your domain's history, DKIM/SPF/DMARC authentication, how often recipients mark similar mail as spam, whether they open it, and content signals. Nobody publishes the algorithm; you see the outcome.

Why it drove the Postmark point: on a shared-IP provider, your inbox placement is hostage to *other customers on the same IPs*. If Brevo's cheap tier carries spammy senders, Gmail learns to distrust those IPs, and your perfectly clean newsletter inherits the penalty — that's the "emails landing in spam" complaint in those reviews. Postmark's whole business is refusing risky senders so their IP pool stays trusted, which is why their placement reputation is the industry benchmark. Resend sits in between: young but developer-heavy customer base, currently well regarded.

For our list specifically, the levers in order of impact: the DKIM/SPF/DMARC records on `ivue.dev` (we set these up during provider onboarding — table stakes), sending only to people who actually signed up (our double-opt-in-able form), the working unsubscribe link (people who can't unsubscribe click "spam" instead — the worst signal you can generate), and steady low-volume cadence rather than sudden blasts. Our drip design is naturally good at all four.

# ivue newsletter Worker

Subscribe endpoint + audience + send ledger (all D1) + daily drip cron.
Postmark delivers the email; this Worker decides who gets what, when.

**The invariant:** at most one email per (subscriber, post), ever. The
`sends` table is the invariant; the drip picks each subscriber's **oldest
unsent** post, so an ad-hoc `/broadcast` today can never be repeated by the
drip later — there is no exclusion logic, just the ledger.

Cadence: one email per subscriber at most every `CADENCE_HOURS` (default
40h ≈ every other day). A broadcast counts as that day's email.

## One-time setup

1. **Postmark account** at postmarkapp.com ($15/mo for 10k emails after
   the ~100-email trial; trial only sends to addresses on your own
   verified domain — perfect for testing this Worker end-to-end free).

   - Add **Sender Signature / domain** `ivue.dev` and set the DKIM +
     Return-Path DNS records it shows (Cloudflare DNS, 5 minutes).
   - In your server, create a **Broadcasts message stream** (newsletters
     must not ride the transactional stream — Postmark enforces this).
     Put its id in `wrangler.jsonc` → `POSTMARK_STREAM` (default id is
     `broadcasts`).
   - Copy the **Server API token** (server → API Tokens).

2. **Create the database and apply the schema** (from this directory):

   ```sh
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 d1 create ivue-newsletter
   #   → paste the printed database_id into wrangler.jsonc
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 d1 execute ivue-newsletter --remote --file=schema.sql
   ```

3. **Secrets:**

   ```sh
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 secret put POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 secret put ADMIN_SECRET   # long random string
   ```

4. **Deploy** (wrangler pinned — see LESSONS.md on 4.121.0):

   ```sh
   npx wrangler@4.120.1 deploy
   ```

   Paste the printed `*.workers.dev` URL into `wrangler.jsonc` →
   `WORKER_ORIGIN` and deploy once more (unsubscribe links embed it).

5. **Point the site form at the Worker:** set `NEWSLETTER_ENDPOINT` in
   `docs_v2/.vitepress/theme/components/NewsletterSignup.vue` to the same
   URL, rebuild, deploy the site.

## Verify before real subscribers

Subscribe with your own address via the site form (or curl), then force a
drip pass instead of waiting for the cron:

```sh
curl -X POST "$WORKER/subscribe" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Evgeny","email":"user@example.com"}'
# dashboard → Workers → ivue-newsletter → Triggers → run cron now
```

Check the email arrives in the INBOX (not spam), the unsubscribe link
works, and the ledger recorded it:

```sh
npx wrangler@4.120.1 d1 execute ivue-newsletter --remote \
  --command='SELECT * FROM sends'
```

## Ad-hoc broadcast (also the future MCP tool surface)

```sh
curl -X POST "$WORKER/broadcast" \
  -H "authorization: [redacted]" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"slug":"circular-imports-dissolved"}'
```

Sends that post now to everyone who never received it, writes the ledger,
and reports `{recipients, skippedAsRepeat}`.

## How the drip finds posts

The site build emits `https://ivue.dev/blog-index.json`
(`docs_v2/scripts/blog-index-generator.mjs`, chained into `build:docs`) —
slugs, titles, descriptions, dates, sorted oldest-first. Publishing a post
requires no Worker change: it appears in the index, and everyone who is
caught up receives it as their next drip email.

## Notes

- Per-message batch outcomes are honored: only `ErrorCode 0` (accepted)
  writes the ledger; rejected recipients are logged and naturally retried
  or surfaced. Postmark's own suppression list (hard bounces, spam
  complaints) blocks on their side in addition to our `unsubscribes`.
- Subscribers live ONLY in D1 — back up with
  `npx wrangler@4.120.1 d1 export ivue-newsletter --remote --output=backup.sql`
  before schema changes.

parts.text: so is cloudflare worker kinda like aws lambda?

Yes — same category (serverless functions: you deploy code, no servers, billed per use), but the execution model is different in ways that matter:

**How they run.** Lambda spins up a **microVM** per concurrent execution — a miniature Linux with your full Node/Python runtime. Workers run your code in **V8 isolates** — the same lightweight sandboxes Chrome uses for tabs — inside an already-running process. That's the root of most practical differences:

- **Cold starts**: Lambda's are tens to hundreds of ms (the VM boots); Workers are effectively zero (~5ms — the isolate just instantiates). Nobody's first request waits.
- **Where it runs**: a Lambda lives in a region you choose (us-east-1…); a Worker deploys to *every* Cloudflare edge location (~300 cities) at once and runs wherever the request lands.
- **Runtime**: Lambda gives you real Node.js (or Python, etc.) — any native module works. Workers give you a browser-like environment: `fetch`, WebCrypto, Web streams — no filesystem, no raw TCP by default, Node APIs only via a compatibility layer. Our newsletter Worker is written entirely against those web standards (that's why it's `fetch()` to Postmark and `crypto.subtle` for the HMAC).
- **Limits**: Lambda can run 15 minutes with gigabytes of RAM — fine for video transcoding. Workers cap *CPU time* (ms-scale, though waiting on `fetch` doesn't count) — built for request/response and light glue, not heavy compute.

**The ecosystem mapping**, since you know AWS: D1 ≈ a tiny built-in RDS/SQLite, KV ≈ DynamoDB-flavored key-value, R2 ≈ S3 (no egress fees), Queues ≈ SQS, Cron Triggers ≈ EventBridge scheduled rules, Durable Objects ≈ nothing AWS quite has (single-instance stateful coordinators).

**Why Workers fit our two uses specifically**: ivue.dev is static assets served at the edge (Lambda would be the wrong tool entirely), and the newsletter Worker is a thin scheduler that mostly *waits* on Postmark and D1 — near-zero CPU, so it lives comfortably inside the free tier where an always-warm Lambda + RDS-shaped setup would cost real money. The general rule: Workers for edge glue and request-shaped logic; Lambda when you need heavy runtimes, native binaries, long computations, or deep AWS integration.

You'd be embedding a worse version of a button your readers already have.

Each `(prototype, key)` gets a fresh `Symbol(key)` during processing, so a base's
`summary` and a child's `summary` cache under different symbols on the same instance.
A child computed can call `super.summary.value` and get the _parent's_ Ref/Computed, not its
own; overrides at different levels cooperate exactly as in native classes.

**Rules out** — `super.x` resolving back to the child's own value (an infinite loop
or the wrong layer); a parent and child sharing a name clobbering each other's cache.

### Deterministic teardown

> The engine installs two helpers per class, once: `$watch` registers watchers in a
> lazily-created per-instance effect scope, and `$stopEffects()` stops that scope,
> runs a user `stopEffects()` hook, and drops every cached Ref/Computed.

`$watch` does `(raw[SCOPE] ??= effectScope(true)).run(() => watch(...))` — the scope
exists only after the first `$watch`. `$stopEffects` runs your hook, stops the scope
if there is one, then deletes every cache symbol (keeping the `RAW` anchor).
Re-accessing a member afterward re-materializes it fresh, and **instances that never
`$watch` allocate no scope at all**.

Why a scope and not `effect.stop()`: in Vue 3.5+ `computed().effect.stop` is gone,
and refs / lazy-computeds are collected once dereferenced. The only thing that
genuinely needs stopping is user watchers — exactly what the scope owns.

# blog-banner — deterministic banners for ivue.dev blog posts

Banners are **code, not paintings**: an HTML/CSS composition rendered
by headless Chromium at exactly 1200×630. Same input → same PNG. No
image model is involved; the source is the artifact.

## Where things live

- **Source of truth**: `.claude/skills/blog-banner/banners/<slug>.html`
  — one file per post, named exactly after the post's slug.
- **Rendered output**: `docs_v2/public/blog/<slug>.png` (referenced by
  the post's `![...](/blog/<slug>.png)` and the index card).
- **Renderer**: `docs_v2/scripts/brand-image-generator.mjs` `blog`
  mode, wrapped as an npm script.

## The pipeline

```bash
npm run render:banner -- \
  .claude/skills/blog-banner/banners/<slug>.html \
  docs_v2/public/blog/<slug>.png
```

The generator waits for fonts and images before screenshotting, so the
render is stable. NEVER hand-run playwright inline for a banner —
the npm script is the reproducibility contract. Commit the HTML source
together with the PNG; a banner whose source is lost cannot be
edited, only replaced.

## Design language (keep banners recognizably one family)

- **Canvas**: `1200×630`, background `#050a18` with two soft radial
  glows — indigo (`rgba(99,102,241,…)`) high, cyan
  (`rgba(34,211,238,…)`) low — plus a faint blue grid masked to the
  center (see any existing banner source for the exact recipe).

# The field, not the rules

<BlogPostDate />

![The field, not the rules](/blog/the-field-not-the-rules.png)

There are two ways to get good code out of a codebase.

The first is **rules**: style guides, review checklists, lint warnings,
onboarding docs. Rules assume the bad moves stay available and ask
everyone, politely and forever, not to make them. Every rule is a
standing tax — it must be taught, remembered, enforced, and re-litigated
in every code review until the end of the project. Rules police a space
that remains dangerous.

The second is **the field**: change what can be expressed, so the bad
moves stop existing as moves. Nobody reviews for the mistake because the
mistake has no syntax. Nobody remembers the discipline because there is
nothing to remember — the shortest path and the correct path are the
same path.

> A convention says "please don't." A field says "there is no such
> move." The first is ethics. The second is physics.

ivue started as a reactivity engine. What it turned into — together with
the invariants built around it — is a field change: a deliberate
reshaping of JavaScript's possibility space, flipping the substrate's
defaults one by one until sound design became the path of least
resistance.

## The inversion table

Each row is one default of stock JavaScript, inverted:

| stock JavaScript defaults to… | the reshaped field defaults to… |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| eager evaluation at module load | nothing exists until first access |
| unbound methods — `this` is the caller's problem | bound methods, stable identity |
| references resolve at import time | references resolve at first touch |
| module-level state as the path of least resistance | state has no legal home outside a class |
| import cycles as runtime landmines | cycles structurally inert |
| caching manual, ad-hoc, everywhere | caching a rare, census-able annotation |

None of these is a rule someone follows. Each is what the code *does*
when nobody is trying. A ref-getter cannot allocate before first read —
laziness is not a discipline, it is the mechanism. An ivue method
arrives bound because the engine binds it at the prototype — passing
`box.grow` as a handler simply works, and the entire class of
`this`-loss bugs becomes unwritable. A cross-module reference inside a
method body resolves when the method runs — long after every module has
loaded — so the [oldest structural wound in
JavaScript](/blog/circular-imports-dissolved) closes not because anyone
is careful but because load-time reads stopped being expressible.

## Enforcement is what makes it a field

Inside [Invar](/examples/invar) — the terminal IDE that AI agents built
on ivue — the inversions are not aspirational. They are gated by AST
checks that run with the test suite: no eager module-level `const`
holding state, no loose functions floating outside classes, no
load-time reads across modules. Everything lives inside classes;
everything defers; everything loads on demand.

That gate is the line between a style and a field. A style guide bends
under deadline pressure — one exception, then five, then the guide is
archaeology. An AST check does not bend. Code that expresses the old
defaults doesn't get merged, so the field's curvature holds at 144,000
lines exactly as it held at ten.

> Constraints you must remember will eventually be forgotten.
> Constraints built into the field cannot be.

The census numbers are what holding looks like: [372 files in a deeply
cyclic domain, zero value-import cycles](/blog/circular-imports-dissolved),
zero `forwardRef`-style workarounds, zero load-order rules. Across the
editor's reactive core, [three `computed()` calls](/engine) — each one a
deliberate, documented purchase. Not because agents were disciplined.
Because the alternatives were not reachable.

## Removing expressiveness — where it was useless

"Less expressive" sounds like a loss. Look at what was actually removed:

- The ability to read another module's value before loading finished.
- The ability to scatter mutable state across module scope.
- The ability to pass a method and silently lose its `this`.
- The ability to allocate reactive machinery for values nobody reads.

Every one of these is **degenerate freedom** — a way to say something
that was never worth saying. No feature was lost; a class of regrets
was. What remains is a smaller language that can express everything the
domain needs and nothing it apologizes for. The same subtraction that
took the engine to [98 lines](/blog/one-kilobyte-feature), applied one
level up — to the possibility space itself.

This is an old idea wearing new tools. Type systems made illegal states
unrepresentable in *data*. The field makes illegal designs
unrepresentable in *architecture* — load order, binding, state
placement, cache policy — the layer where projects actually rot.

## Why agents thrive on it

The strangest evidence came from watching the fleet work.
[Agents produced patterns the author never wrote](/blog/patterns-the-author-never-wrote) —
capability classes, reactive control planes, structures no example ever
showed them. That is not obedience. Obedience reproduces the training
examples; it does not exceed them.

The explanation is the field. An agent exploring a rule-based codebase
must model the rules *and* the ways they bend — its search space is full
of moves that compile today and rot tomorrow. An agent exploring a
constrained field can search **aggressively**, because every reachable
point is structurally sound. Constrain the space and exploration becomes
safe; make exploration safe and you get emergence instead of entropy.

> Rules cap how bad the code can get. A field raises how good it can
> get — by making the search space safe to explore at full speed.

That inversion — constraints as an accelerant, not a brake — is the part
worth sitting with. The [AI-era argument](/blog/reactive-framework-for-the-ai-era)
usually stops at "agents need guardrails." The field goes further:
agents need a *geometry*, and given one, they build things their
operators didn't specify and couldn't have. The proof is not a claim
about the future. It is [running software](/examples/invar).

## The claim, plainly

We did not write better JavaScript. We changed what JavaScript defaults
to — evaluation time, binding, state placement, resolution order — and
then removed the expressiveness that only ever produced regret. The
game plays differently because the board is shaped differently.

Rules are what you need when the field is wrong. Fix the field, and the
rules dissolve into it — unenforced, unremembered, and unbroken.

Start with [What is ivue?](/guide/introduction), see the defaults up
close in the [Standard](/guide/standard), or read what this field made
[buildable](/blog/what-becomes-buildable).

structured.stdout:
## `Static()` — the static-side sibling (from `ivue/extras`)

`Reactive()` owns instances. Stateless CAPABILITY classes — function bags for
files, git, parsers, clocks: never constructed, only called and swapped — use
`Static()` from the `ivue/extras` entry (separate, so core stays the engine):

- **Static methods bind lazily with stable identity** — detachable, safe as a
  router/queue/listener callback, bound to the RECEIVING class.
- **Get-only statics named `$…` compute once PER RECEIVER.** The `$` prefix
  promises stable identity, NOT immutability — a mutable memo table is a
  legitimate `$`-cache. Non-`$` static getters stay LIVE: those are the knobs
  test subclasses pinch.

THE ANCHOR RULE — a class that declares static members wraps them ONCE, at
`$Class`, so subclasses and test doubles inherit working semantics by
extending `$Class` bare:

```ts
import { Static } from 'ivue/extras';

class $GitCommands {
  static get binary() {
    return 'git'; // LIVE knob — no $ prefix
  }
  static get $environment() {
    return { LC_ALL: 'C' }; // computed once per receiver
  }
  static stage(path: string) {
    return this.run(['add', '--', path]); // `this` = receiving class
  }
}

export namespace GitCommands {
  export const $Class = Static($GitCommands); // anchor — wrap HERE
  export let Class = $Class; // selection — kernels/tests swap this
}
```

Statics AND reactive instances on one class — anchor the statics, then
`Reactive()`:


parts.text:
Fixed (`2efaf7b`). Here's the full picture of what was breaking and what now catches it:

**The mechanism**: VitePress splits every page into content-hashed chunks (`blog.abc123.js`). A deploy replaces the whole asset set atomically, so the old hashes stop existing. A visitor whose tab loaded the *previous* build clicks to another page → the SPA router dynamic-imports a chunk by its old hash → 404 → the navigation dies silently. That's why the blog "didn't load" until a manual refresh: the refresh is what fetched the new HTML with the new chunk graph.

**The fix**: Vite fires a `vite:preloadError` window event on precisely this failure. The theme now listens and does what the user would do by hand — `location.reload()` — which lands them on the new build at the URL they were navigating to. One stutter instead of a dead page, and only for tabs that were open across a deploy. Verified the handler ships in the built bundle (it's in the theme chunk).

**Why this is the whole fix and not half of one**: your `_headers` were already correct — HTML at `max-age=0, must-revalidate` (so the reload is guaranteed to fetch fresh HTML, not a cached old copy) and hashed assets immutable. And Cloudflare Workers assets deploys are atomic with automatic edge invalidation, so there's no stale-edge problem like the GitHub Pages days — no append-only tricks needed. The only unclosable window was the already-open tab, which is exactly what the event handler closes.

This goes live on your next push — and note the fix protects tabs opened *after* that deploy; tabs currently open on today's production build predate the handler, so they'll break one last time on the deploy that ships it.
